title: Is Europe’s gas market inching towards a winter crisis? | Wood Mackenzie
gist: European spot gas is trading above €60/MWh (US$20/mmbtu), more than 50% above the level at the 12 June US–Iran MoU signing, because Strait of Hormuz shipping has halted again while EU storage sits just above 50% full and Asian demand has recovered to 2025 levels. Wood Mackenzie's Massimo Di Odoardo argues European storage reaches at most 75% by 1 November versus a 90% five-year average, locking in elevated prices through winter 2026/27, yet still expects an over-supplied LNG market from 2028 given 250+ Mtpa under construction.

themes.theme: Hormuz re-closure and the gas price spike

insights.claim: European spot gas prices are trading above €60/MWh (US$20/mmbtu), more than 50% higher than at the signing of the US–Iran Memorandum of Understanding on 12 June 2026, after military strikes resumed and Strait of Hormuz shipping largely ground to a halt again.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The MoU rally in gas has fully unwound — positioning for a Hormuz de-escalation trade in European gas has been a losing carry so far.
insights.quote: European spot prices are currently trading above €60/MWh (US$20/mmbtu), reaching heights last seen at the start of the conflict as winter ended, and more than 50% higher than at the signing of the MoU.
insights.locator: Hopes that the war in the Middle East might end

insights.claim: Gas prices are reacting more violently than Brent crude to the renewed Middle East disruption, making European gas the higher-beta expression of Hormuz risk.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: For geopolitical risk expression, TTF/JKM offers more convexity per unit of Hormuz headline than crude.
insights.quote: Gas prices are proving more sensitive than Brent.
insights.locator: Gas prices are proving more sensitive than Brent

insights.claim: The US–Iran Memorandum of Understanding signed on 12 June 2026 has not restored energy flows, with both sides ratcheting military strikes back up and optimism about reopening the Strait of Hormuz proving short-lived.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Diplomatic headlines are not a durable signal for de-risking energy exposure — trade physical flows, not MoUs.
insights.locator: Hopes that the war in the Middle East might end

themes.theme: Three structural amplifiers behind the price move

insights.claim: European gas storage is only just above 50% full, a historically low level for late July, raising the risk that Europe cannot refill enough gas ahead of the 2026/27 winter heating season.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Storage percentage is the single cleanest weekly indicator for whether the winter 2026/27 gas curve keeps steepening.
insights.quote: European gas storage is only just above 50% full, an historically low level at this time of the year

insights.claim: Asian LNG demand has rebounded since April 2026 and is back at 2025 levels despite the shortfall of Qatari volumes and firm prices, intensifying competition with Europe for marginal cargoes.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Asian price-elasticity has been weaker than assumed — the JKM–TTF spread is the mechanism that decides who gets winter cargoes.
insights.quote: Asian demand has rebounded since April and is now back at 2025 levels, despite the shortfall of Qatari volumes and firm prices.

insights.claim: There are limited additional LNG supply volumes arriving over the next 9 to 12 months, with new Qatari developments now expected to start up only in the second half of 2027.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: No supply-side relief valve exists before H2 2027, so the tightness has to clear through price and demand destruction rather than new molecules.
insights.quote: There are limited additional volumes of LNG supply coming to market over the next 9 to 12 months, with new Qatari developments now only expected to start up in the second half of 2027.

insights.claim: Even in a best case where Qatar restarts and reaches full operational capacity by end-September 2026 excluding its two damaged trains, European gas storage will reach at most 75% of capacity by 1 November — well below the 90% five-year average going into winter.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Even the bullish-resolution scenario leaves a 15-point storage deficit, which caps how far the winter curve can sell off on good news.
insights.quote: we estimate that European storage will only reach 75% capacity at best by 1 November. That’s well below the 90% average of the past five years ahead of winter.
insights.locator: How does the Strait of Hormuz play into this?

insights.claim: When Strait of Hormuz flows resume, European gas prices should drop initially, but low storage inventories almost guarantee elevated prices through winter 2026/27 and into 2027.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A reopening headline is a short-lived selling opportunity, not a regime change — fade the first spike down in winter gas.
insights.quote: As flows resume through the Strait, we would expect prices to drop initially. However, low storage inventories almost guarantee elevated prices through this winter and into 2027.
insights.locator: How does the Strait of Hormuz play into this?

insights.claim: If the Strait of Hormuz closure is extended by another two months, European storage would struggle to reach even 70% of capacity before winter, driving prices higher still as Europe competes with Asia for limited cargoes.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Each additional month of closure maps to roughly 2-3 points of lost European storage — a tradeable rule of thumb for sizing tail risk.
insights.quote: European storage levels would struggle to reach even 70% capacity were closure to be extended by another two months.

insights.claim: Wealthier European and Asian countries will buy their way through the winter while some emerging Asian economies inevitably face demand destruction as LNG becomes unaffordable.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Price-sensitive South and Southeast Asian buyers are the marginal balancing item — watch their cargo cancellations as the release valve that caps the rally.
insights.quote: some emerging Asian economies will inevitably face demand destruction as LNG becomes increasingly unaffordable

insights.claim: European gas prices remain nowhere near the levels reached after Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the loss of Russian pipeline supply, so the current episode is not a repeat of 2022 at least not yet.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sets the ceiling for the current move — 2022 highs are the reference point, and the market is still well short of them.
insights.quote: This isn’t 2022 all over again – at least not yet.

insights.claim: The knock-on effects of high gas prices on European power markets are less severe than in 2022 because of the policy response since then and the huge investment in renewables capacity.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The gas-to-power pass-through coefficient has structurally fallen — European utilities and power offtakers are less exposed to a gas spike than the 2022 analogue implies.
insights.quote: the implications for European power markets are now less severe, given the policy response since 2022 and the huge levels of investment in renewables capacity since

insights.claim: Europe is nonetheless approaching energy crisis territory, and there are limited alternatives to gas today despite long-term policy goals, meaning urgent short-term action is needed to reduce market risk.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The gap between EU long-term electrification targets and near-term physical gas dependence is where policy surprises will come from.
insights.quote: Nevertheless, Europe is approaching energy crisis territory.

insights.claim: The EU last week launched an Electrification Action Plan aimed at almost doubling electrification by 2040 and cutting gas demand by 65% to 70% over the same period, framed as a response to the Gulf war and import dependence.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A structural demand-side headwind for long-dated European gas and a policy tailwind for electrification equipment, grids and heat pumps.
insights.quote: the EU last week launched its hugely ambitious Electrification Action Plan aimed at almost doubling electrification by 2040 and reducing gas demand by 65% to 70% in the same period

insights.claim: If winter 2026/27 becomes critical, the EU may be forced to rethink two supply-constraining energy policies: more stringent methane emission regulations and the ban on all Russian LNG imports from January 2027.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A rollback or delay of the January 2027 Russian LNG ban is an underpriced bearish catalyst for European gas — watch Brussels rhetoric as storage numbers land.
insights.quote: the EU might well be forced to rethink two of its key energy policy goals that could constrain imports: rolling out more stringent methane emission regulations and banning all Russian LNG imports from January 2027
insights.locator: If the coming winter situation becomes critical

insights.claim: Crises and government responses tend to be defined by their immediate impact rather than long-term goals, which is why Europe's 2040 targets do not solve a 2026/27 winter problem.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A mental model for reading EU energy policy: near-term scarcity, not decarbonisation targets, drives what actually gets legislated.
insights.quote: But crises – and governments’ responses to them – tend to be defined by their immediate impact.

insights.claim: With over 250 Mtpa of new LNG supply under construction, an over-supplied global LNG market from 2028 remains the most likely outcome despite the current squeeze.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The long-dated bearish LNG thesis is intact — the trade is a steep backwardation, not a parallel shift up in the curve.
insights.quote: with over 250 Mtpa of new LNG supply under construction, an over-supplied LNG market from 2028 remains the most likely outcome
insights.locator: Are we still heading into an over-supplied market?

insights.claim: If the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted or new risks emerge, both the duration and depth of the expected post-2028 LNG over-supply could prove less significant than currently assumed.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The consensus 2028 glut is conditional on geopolitical normalisation — a persistent Hormuz risk premium would revalue LNG developers and long-dated contracts.
insights.quote: If the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted or new risks emerge, however, both the duration and depth of LNG over-supply could prove less significant.
insights.locator: Are we still heading into an over-supplied market?

insights.claim: The resilience of global LNG supply is poised to be tested to its limits over the next 6 to 12 months.
insights.speaker: Massimo Di Odoardo, VP Gas and LNG Research, Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Outage and force-majeure headlines from any major liquefaction hub now carry outsized price impact given zero spare supply.
insights.quote: The resilience of LNG supply is poised to be tested to the limits over the next 6 to 12 months.
insights.locator: Are we still heading into an over-supplied market?
